case_studies.title: ProLog — Mobile Apprenticeship Companion
case_studies.subtitle: A journey companion for neurodivergent apprentices
case_studies.summary: A centralized apprenticeship companion helping neurodivergent apprentices track progress, reduce cognitive overload, and build confidence through clear visualization and structured tools.

evidence_narrative.original_assumption: Recreating the full apprenticeship system in-app would stay manageable day to day.
evidence_narrative.research_changed_direction: Policy review and stakeholder interviews showed fragmented status tracking created high cognitive load, especially for neurodivergent apprentices.
evidence_narrative.what_changed_why: Because users needed immediate orientation, we moved to a dashboard-first flow that unified progress, discrepancies, and next steps.
evidence_narrative.next_iteration: Measure time-to-report and discrepancy-flow completion with active apprentices in moderated tests.

case_studies.context: School project in collaboration with ConnectHER at BCIT

hook.content: Apprenticeship can take over 6,000 hours. That's years of work spread across job sites, classrooms, and bureaucratic systems — often without a clear sense of whether you're on track.

media_demo.caption: Dashboard-first entry reduces cross-system status hunting by surfacing progress and next steps immediately.

launch_ad.title: ProLog Launch Media
launch_ad.caption: Short walkthrough of the problem, process, and final ProLog flow.

problem_framing.content:
Apprentices in British Columbia navigate a fragmented system: hours in one tool, competencies in another, and certification requirements buried in dense PDFs.

Because status checks required cross-referencing multiple sources, routine progress verification became slow and error-prone. For neurodivergent apprentices, that switching cost increased cognitive load and reduced completion confidence.

The design goal became clear: reduce cross-system hunting and make next steps visible in one place.

methods: Persona development based on lived experience
Team reflection sessions that included neurodivergent members
key_findings: Progress tracking is scattered across multiple platforms with no single source of truth
Official systems are desktop-first and difficult to use on job sites
Discrepancies between employer-logged and self-logged hours create anxiety
Neurodivergent users experience amplified cognitive load from inconsistent interfaces

do.title: Do
do.rule: Map fragmented systems into one clear progress model users can scan in seconds.
do.illustrationText: Single source of truth for hours and competencies

dont.title: Don't
dont.rule: Don't mirror the original bureaucracy inside the product interface.

media_demo.caption: Research findings were translated into one hierarchy that prioritizes status checks and discrepancy actions.

lofi_phase.content:
Early sketches tested one question: what must an apprentice see in the first three seconds to trust their status?

Because policy-first layouts buried action details, the structure shifted to dashboard-first with progress, discrepancies, and next-step prompts at the top.

Lower-priority utilities stayed secondary until the core orientation flow worked reliably.

prototype.description: Mid-fi walkthrough for early structure and hierarchy decisions.

before.caption: Before: dashboard sections competed for attention, slowing status checks.

after.caption: After: stronger hierarchy and contrast made progress status and next actions faster to scan.

before.caption: Before: finance support appeared as dense text blocks with weak grouping.

after.caption: After: grouped funding sections improved scanability and reduced lookup effort.

before.caption: Before: quiz-prep progress cues were compact and easy to miss.

after.alt: ProLog hi-fi competency exam prep screen
after.caption: After: dedicated quiz-prep flow clarified pacing and made study status easier to track.

hifi_phase.content:
Because testing showed users needed fast orientation, the hi-fi phase prioritized calm hierarchy over decorative density. Typography, spacing, and contrast were tuned so progress, discrepancies, and next steps stayed scannable on job-site breaks.

The dashboard remained the anchor, with secondary utilities visually deprioritized to protect decision speed.

prototype.description: Hi-fi walkthrough focused on final interface polish and flow.

before.caption: Before: progress and reminders were present but visual priority was uneven.

after.caption: After: typography and spacing established clearer priority for progress checks.

before.caption: Before: resources relied on text-heavy blocks with limited section separation.

after.caption: After: stronger grouping and spacing improved retrieval of funding details.

before.caption: Before: competency progress was visible but lacked explicit study-flow guidance.

after.alt: ProLog hi-fi competency exam prep screen
after.caption: After: exam-prep cues made competency progression and next steps more explicit.

images.caption: Dashboard view prioritizes current status, reducing time spent checking progress across systems.
Discrepancy workflow helps users identify and report hour mismatches with less ambiguity.
Quiz-prep screen supports exam readiness with clear competency-linked practice prompts.

feature_breakdown.intro: Each feature addresses one concrete friction point. Explore the prototype to see how they connect.

features.title: Progress Dashboard
features.description: A centralized view of hours completed, competencies achieved, and certification progress. Current status is visible within one tap.
features.why: Apprentices reported feeling lost in fragmented systems. The dashboard provides constant orientation without extra navigation.
features.caption: Dashboard overview with hours, milestones, and next steps.

features.title: Hours Discrepancy Detector
features.description: Compares user-logged hours against official records and flags mismatches. Users can document and report discrepancies directly.
features.why: Hour disputes are stressful and common. The feature provides clear tools for reporting and resolution.
features.caption: Hours discrepancy and logging view.

features.title: Financial Resources Hub
features.description: Links to grants, funding programs, and cost breakdowns for apprenticeship expenses — all in one place.
features.why: Financial stress appeared consistently in research. The feature improves visibility and access to available support pathways.
features.caption: Funding and support resources grouped into one screen.

features.title: AI Practice Quizzes
features.description: Generates practice questions based on trade competencies to build confidence before official exams.
features.why: Many apprentices feel underprepared for certification. Low-stakes practice reduces that anxiety.
features.caption: Quiz prep flow with competency-aligned practice prompts.

prototype.description: Walk through each feature. Start with the dashboard, then explore the hours tracker and quiz flow.

do.title: Do
do.rule: Tie every feature to one concrete user anxiety and make the payoff explicit.

dont.title: Don't
dont.rule: Don't ship utility features that lack a direct apprenticeship outcome.

media_demo.caption: Feature set prioritizes orientation, discrepancy confidence, and exam readiness.

validation.content:
Validation checked whether participants could confirm status and act on discrepancies without facilitator help.

Because users quickly located hour status and repeatedly identified discrepancy tracking as the most useful flow, the dashboard-first structure and reporting path were retained.

Feedback then informed copy and hierarchy refinements in final screens.
outcomes: Participants found current hour status quickly without searching multiple systems.
The discrepancy tracker was repeatedly identified as the most useful workflow.
Dashboard structure made progress checks feel clearer and more reliable.

media_demo.caption: Validation confirmed users could verify status and act on discrepancies with less uncertainty.

what_i_learned.reflection: When users said they felt 'relieved,' they were responding to design decisions—not just information architecture.

what_i_learned.insight: Scope control is a design skill
what_i_learned.reflection: Saying no to good ideas was harder than coming up with them.
Seeing how far you've come matters as much as knowing what's next.
Student projects do not always have access to large sample sizes. That limitation does not invalidate qualitative insights.

case_studies.title: InkLink — Collaborative Writing App
case_studies.subtitle: Breaking writer's block through collaboration
case_studies.summary: A chain-writing platform that reduces writer's block by turning writing into a shared, low-pressure activity where users contribute one passage at a time.

evidence_narrative.original_assumption: Mobile-first with many features would best support collaborative writing.
evidence_narrative.research_changed_direction: Usability tests showed longer drafting worked better on larger screens with clearer story context.
evidence_narrative.what_changed_why: Because contributors needed reading clarity first, we shifted to a desktop-first flow and reduced competing actions.
evidence_narrative.next_iteration: Measure contribution completion and return-session starts after collaboration-cue updates.

responsibilities: Led user research and concept validation

hero.marqueeText: CÅSE STUDIËS • INKLINK • COLLABORATIVE WRITING APP

hook.content:
Everyone has a story they never finished.

Ideas were there. Momentum wasn't.

InkLink started with one question: what if writing felt shared instead of solitary?

media_demo.caption: Hero feed reduces first-action friction by surfacing active stories and one clear join path.

launch_ad.title: InkLink Launch Media
launch_ad.caption: Promo video plus slide walkthrough of the problem, process, and final InkLink flow.

problem_framing.content:
Writer's block usually comes from pressure, not a lack of ideas. The blank page, perfection expectations, and solo ownership of every next sentence can stall momentum.

The design direction focused on removing those barriers by making writing collaborative instead of solitary.

methods: Peer surveys with amateur and hobbyist writers
Concept validation sessions to gauge interest
key_findings: Most creative writing happens on desktop or tablet—not mobile phones
Dense, text-heavy layouts discourage reading and contribution
New concepts require gentle onboarding; users won't explore without guidance

do.title: Do
do.rule: Prioritize scan-friendly structure and clear contribution prompts.

dont.title: Don't
dont.rule: Avoid dense copy blocks that raise cognitive load before writing starts.

media_demo.caption: Research-led concept reduced entry hesitation by emphasizing one primary contribution action.

lofi_phase.content:
Lo-fi exploration tested one core behavior: contribute without losing story context.

Because dense layouts reduced reading completion in early tests, the interaction model shifted toward clearer story structure, lighter prompts, and fewer competing actions.

Visual polish was deferred until the contribution flow could be completed quickly and consistently.

prototype.description: Temporary lo-fi reference sourced from the existing InkLink test artifact.

feature_breakdown.intro: InkLink focuses on three core collaboration flows. Explore them in the prototype below.

features.title: Public Story Chains
features.description: Open stories that anyone can contribute to. Writers join, add a passage, and pass the story forward.
features.why: Low barrier to entry. No commitment required—just jump in and write.
features.caption: Feed view solves discovery friction with scannable story entries and clear join actions.

features.title: Private Writing Circles
features.description: Invite-only spaces for friends or writing groups. Turn order is set by the creator.
features.why: Some writers want collaboration without strangers. Private circles offer that control.
features.caption: Private-circle view clarifies turn ownership and contribution status to reduce coordination confusion.

features.title: Timed Contributions
features.description: Optional time limits encourage momentum. If a turn expires, the next writer can step in.
features.why: Deadlines reduce overthinking. A 24-hour window is long enough to be fair, short enough to keep stories moving.
features.caption: Timed editor state protects momentum with explicit turn limits and submission feedback.

prototype.description: Explore the feature set in the same hi-fi prototype flow used across the case study.

do.title: Do
do.rule: Design each mode with one obvious next step so users can start writing immediately.

dont.title: Don't
dont.rule: Don't overload the first screen with options, filters, and setup complexity.

media_demo.caption: Editor interaction keeps contribution lightweight, lowering hesitation before writing.

validation.content:
Validation focused on whether contributors could join, read context, and submit with minimal guidance.

Because participants completed the join-to-submit flow without facilitator help and reported lower hesitation with shared authorship, the simplified CTA structure and timed-turn model were retained.

Final adjustments focused on copy clarity and collaboration cues.
outcomes: Participants could join a chain and submit a turn without facilitator help.
Shared authorship reduced hesitation compared with solo drafting.
Timed turns helped maintain story momentum during tests.

what_i_learned.reflection: Limiting options (one clear CTA, timed turns) reduced friction instead of adding it.
The newspaper aesthetic was fun but counterproductive.
More features were removed than added, and the product improved through that reduction.

hifi_phase.content:
Because testing showed reading clarity drove contribution confidence, the hi-fi phase translated validated flows into a calmer editorial system.

Typography, spacing, and hierarchy emphasized story progression and next action, while secondary controls were de-emphasized.

The final visual language preserved personality without competing with writing tasks.

prototype.description: Temporary hi-fi walkthrough sourced from the current InkLink final prototype.

images.alt: InkLink hi-fi home and story feed
images.caption: Hi-fi home view prioritizes readable story scanning and clear contribution entry points.
The reading view keeps contributor context and next-action prompts visible while scrolling.
The editor reduces friction with focused writing space and lightweight status feedback.

media_demo.caption: Final visual language emphasizes flow, readability, and low-pressure contribution.

case_studies.title: SideQuest — Micro-Adventure Web App
case_studies.subtitle: Turning boredom into micro-adventures
case_studies.summary: A web app that helps users discover small, low-commitment activities to break routine, reframing free time as an opportunity rather than a void to fill.

evidence_narrative.original_assumption: Broad filters and upfront controls would improve confidence.
evidence_narrative.research_changed_direction: Usability tests showed option-heavy entry screens increased hesitation before first action.
evidence_narrative.what_changed_why: Because users needed momentum over setup, we reduced the flow to one primary action with clearer quest framing.
what_was_cut: High-friction setup and deep filter stacks
evidence_narrative.next_iteration: A/B test quest messaging and completion prompts for higher browse-to-start conversion.

hook.content: A free afternoon can quickly turn into prolonged scrolling and indecision. SideQuest reframes that moment with one guided next step so users can start an activity with low effort.

media_demo.caption: Hook screen reframes idle time into one low-pressure next action to reduce decision fatigue.

launch_ad.title: SideQuest Launch Media
launch_ad.caption: Slide walkthrough of the problem, process, and final SideQuest flow.

problem_framing.content:
The core problem was decision fatigue, not lack of options. When too many choices appeared at once, participants delayed action and defaulted to passive scrolling.

Because both persona narratives showed this hesitation pattern, the design direction prioritized guided momentum over broad browsing.

Up-front decisions were reduced so users could start with one clear quest action.

methods: Persona creation based on peer interviews (Scout and Goobert archetypes)
Iterative usability testing from low-fi through high-fi screens
Competitive analysis of activity discovery apps
key_findings: Users preferred low-pressure activities that required minimal planning
Choice overload frequently delayed first action
Participants responded positively to guided, single-next-step flows

do.title: Do
do.rule: Reduce choice overload with a guided default that gets users moving quickly.

dont.title: Don't
dont.rule: Don't force users through heavy setup before they see their first useful suggestion.

media_demo.caption: Research findings drove a quick-start flow that removed high-friction setup decisions.

lofi_phase.content:
Early wireframes exposed location, duration, cost, and category controls in the first step.

Because testing showed option-heavy entry screens increased hesitation before first action, the primary path was reduced to one dominant action: "Get a quest."

Secondary controls were moved out of the first screen to protect momentum.

prototype.description: Lo-fi walkthrough showing early quest-discovery structure and simplified action flow.

images.caption: Initial designs with too many options

hifi_phase.content:
Because usability sessions favored fast starts over deep setup, the hi-fi phase kept interaction weight low and concentrated emphasis on quest cards and primary actions.

Playful language and mascot cues supported orientation, while surrounding interface chrome remained restrained.

This preserved a light tone without slowing first action.

images.caption: Home screen centers one quest action so users can start without browsing loops.
Quest cards surface effort and time cues to support faster activity selection.
Detail screen provides only the information needed to begin, reducing planning overhead.
Completion state reinforces progress and supports repeat engagement.

prototype.description: Hi-fi walkthrough across key SideQuest flows and final interaction states.

feature_breakdown.intro: SideQuest centers on three core elements. Explore each in the prototype below.

features.title: Quest Suggestions
features.description: Low-commitment activities framed as optional adventures — each with a title, brief description, and estimated time.
features.why: The word "quest" makes mundane activities feel interesting. Framing matters more than content.
features.caption: Quest cards prioritized by effort and time-to-start.

features.title: Friendly Guide
features.description: A small mascot that appears throughout the experience, offering encouragement without being intrusive.
features.why: The mascot adds warmth. It makes the app feel like a companion, not a tool.
features.caption: Mascot guidance appears at decision points to reduce hesitation.

features.title: Quick Start Flow
features.description: A quest in two taps. No account required, no preferences to configure.
features.why: Each extra step between initial boredom and first activity selection can reduce momentum. The flow minimizes that gap.
features.caption: Two-tap flow from idle state to first quest selection.

prototype.description: Explore quest browsing, selection, and completion states in the hi-fi flow.

do.title: Do
do.rule: Keep language playful and actionable so users commit before overthinking.

dont.title: Don't
dont.rule: Don't over-index on filters and options that delay momentum.

media_demo.caption: Core features prioritize immediacy: pick a quest, start, and continue.

validation.content:
Validation tested whether the simplified flow and quest framing helped users start activities faster.

Because participants interpreted mascot prompts as supportive and completed the two-tap path with less hesitation, the simplified hierarchy and wording were retained.

Findings then informed final copy refinements and feedback-state clarity.
outcomes: Participants described quest framing as approachable and easy to understand.
Mascot-led prompts were interpreted as supportive rather than intrusive.
The two-tap quest flow reduced hesitation before picking an activity.

media_demo.caption: Validation confirmed simplified framing reduced hesitation before first quest selection.

what_i_learned.reflection: Getting users to take one clear first step can be more valuable than exposing many options at once.
Interface elements either build confidence or introduce friction in early decisions.

what_i_learned.insight: Research, design, and code inform each other
what_i_learned.reflection: Close alignment between research, design, and implementation improved decision quality across iterations.
